HomeEssentials Inc. - Q2 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeEssentials Inc. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeEssentials Inc.'s results for the Q2 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Hargrove, Chief Executive Officer; and Sarah Thompson, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Hargrove.

Mike Hargrove, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeEssentials Inc.'s performance for the Q2 2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover four key aspects of our performance:

1. Overall Performance: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for being here for HomeEssentials Inc.'s second quarter fiscal 2024 earnings discussion. Before diving deeper, let me outline the highlights of our overall company performance, which demonstrate resilient execution amid ongoing inflation pressures, declining consumer confidence, and cautious spending on discretionary items—patterns mirrored by peers such as Target and Kohl's.

On the top line, we posted Q2 net sales of $2.85 billion, a 4.2% increase year-over-year that exceeded the midpoint of our guidance and extended our streak to six straight quarters of revenue growth. This momentum stemmed from a 3.8% rise in comparable store sales—our best Q2 showing since 2019—powered by 2.1% higher traffic and a 1.6% boost in average ticket size. Our value-focused merchandise in apparel and home essentials struck a chord, as private-label items from our 'Everyday Forge' basics collection surged 15% year-over-year, pulling market share away from national brands amid budget-conscious buying.

By category, performance was as follows: Apparel and accessories delivered +5.2% comps, spearheaded by +12% growth in women's activewear and men's denim, aided by our precise markdown approach that limited clearance stock to only 8% of inventory—far below the sector norm of 12-15%. Home goods and furniture saw +2.9% comps, with softlines such as bedding climbing 7%, though partially offset by a 1% decline in large-ticket durables due to high interest rates dampening big buys, echoing issues at RH and Williams-Sonoma. Electronics and appliances were essentially flat at +0.1% comps, steadied by deals on mid-range TVs and compact appliances, where Nielsen data shows we captured an extra 200 basis points of share.

Digital channels made up 18% of total revenue, rising from 15% a year earlier, but our omnichannel prowess truly shone through: Buy Online, Pick Up In-Store orders jumped 28% year-over-year, accounting for more than 40% of online sales and elevating in-store conversion by 15%.

Turning to profitability, adjusted gross margin widened by 110 basis points to 32.4%, the strongest Q2 figure in five years. Key factors included reduced freight and shrinkage expenses (down 40 basis points to 1.2% of sales) following RFID implementation in 70% of our 1,250 stores; a richer product mix with private labels now comprising 42% of sales, up from 38%; and savvy sourcing from Southeast Asia suppliers, which offset 20% of rising ocean freight costs.

SG&A expenses as a percentage of sales improved 80 basis points to 24.1%, driven by payroll efficiencies from our AI scheduling system, which trimmed labor hours per store by 4% while holding Net Promoter Scores steady at 78. Together, these improvements yielded adjusted EBITDA of $285 million, a 12% year-over-year gain with a 10.0% margin that topped our long-term goal of 9-10%. Diluted EPS reached $0.72, up 15%, supported by free cash flow of $210 million that funded $150 million in share buybacks under our $1 billion program.

Our physical store network continues to thrive as the foundation of our model: average sales productivity per door climbed 5% to $1.2 million annualized. We added 12 new locations averaging 45,000 square feet in fast-growing Sunbelt areas, relocated three lagging sites, and closed five small-format stores in sparse Northeast urban zones—for a net gain of 8 doors, bringing us to 1,258 total.

Foot traffic data from Placer.ai indicated a 3% year-over-year increase, enhanced by digital features like curbside pickup that extended customer dwell time by 12%.

Regionally, results highlighted our diversification benefits: Sunbelt states (Texas, Florida, Southeast) generated 42% of sales with +6.5% comps, propelled by population shifts and tourism strength—Florida units averaged +9% on beachwear and patio items. Midwest and Plains areas, 28% of sales, posted +4.1% comps, holding firm on essentials despite farm commodity swings. Northeast and West Coast, 30% of sales, managed +1.2% comps, hampered by atypical cool and wet weather (much like Dick's Sporting Goods noted) and high urban office vacancies over 20%, with California flat from Proposition 12 apparel sourcing expenses.

On the technology front, we're fortifying our brick-and-mortar advantage. The 'StoreOS' platform, operational in 500 stores, employs computer vision for 99.5% inventory accuracy and tailored digital signage in-store, increasing add-on purchases by 8%. Symbotic robot pilots for stocking aim for 20% labor reductions by fiscal 2025.

We're also emphasizing experiential shopping: 25% of stores now host 'Hearth Hubs'—compact zones for artisan demonstrations and AR furniture try-ons, akin to IKEA but for mid-tier customers. Our BrickLane Rewards program—rebranded as HomeEssentials Rewards—reached 35 million members, up 18% year-over-year, with a 62% redemption rate doubling lifetime customer value.

In a backdrop of slowing GDP growth projected at 1.8% for the second half per the Fed, we're emphasizing affordability, fluid omnichannel experiences, and targeted capital spending of $450-500 million for fiscal 2024. This setup equips us to outpace the field as shoppers shift from luxury outlets like Macy's toward our everyday low pricing.

2. Regional performance variations: As our brick-and-mortar network of over 1,200 stores nationwide accounts for 78% of total revenue, regional differences were a standout feature this quarter. While we achieved company-wide comparable store sales, or comps, of +4.2%—surpassing the retail sector's +2.8% average according to NRF figures—disparities emerged due to economic pressures, weather variability, competition, and our focused omnichannel efforts.

Breaking it down across our four main U.S. regions—Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, and West—here are the comps, traffic trends, average basket shifts, drivers, and our response strategies.

In the Northeast, representing 22% of our stores and 18% of sales, comps reached +1.8%, trailing the average because of a slow spring from unusually cool, rainy conditions that hurt outdoor categories like patio furniture and grills—traffic fell 3% against our company +1.2% gain. Average unit retail stayed at $48.50, but conversion slipped to 28.5% from 30.1% last year as buyers postponed major purchases amid local inflation at 3.9% CPI per BLS data. Rivals like Home Depot's lumber price cuts and Lowe's big-box push kept our market share steady at 14.2%. On the upside, our Essentials Rewards loyalty drove 15% more repeat visits, and BOPIS—now 22% of transactions—eased traffic weakness.

The Southeast, with 28% of stores and 25% of sales, led strongly at +9.4% comps—over twice the national benchmark. Favorable weather and strong employment (3.1% unemployment versus the U.S. 3.8%) sparked 7.2% traffic growth, especially in Florida and Georgia. Kitchen and bath sales soared +18% with broader quartz countertop and smart appliance selections, tracking housing trends like those at Williams-Sonoma. Average basket rose to $62.30, up 6.8%, aided by bundling with seasonal items like storm prep kits. Inventory turnover hit 5.2x from 4.7x, courtesy of micro-fulfillment hubs in Atlanta and Charlotte that slashed out-of-stocks 40% and supported same-day curbside.

Midwest results, 25% of stores and 27% of sales, were steady at +5.1% comps, backed by durable spending in agricultural states like Illinois and Ohio where corn prices rose 12%. Traffic increased 3.4%, strong in storage and organization goods up 14% for hybrid work adaptations. Shrink climbed to 1.8% of sales from 1.5%, due to theft in cities like Chicago similar to Target's Q1 issues, but our Zebra Technologies AI partnership cut incidents 22% in test stores. Gross margins grew 110 basis points to 42.3% from cheaper freight via regional DCs.

The West, 25% of stores and 30% of sales, mixed at +2.9% comps, dragged by California's living costs and weak luxury demand—high-end bedding and decor down 8% after tech layoffs at Google and Meta. Traffic edged +0.4%, but conversion rose to 32.1% up 210 basis points via app-tied digital kiosks, pushing AUR to $55.20. Wildfires in Colorado and Oregon disrupted chains, lifting inventory 5% to 12 weeks, but direct vendor ties like Mohawk Flooring held margins at 41.1%—behind Walmart's +4.5% but ahead of Macy's city woes.

Broader patterns show Sun Belt outperformance versus traditional markets, matching 1.2 million net southern migrations per 2023 Census data. Firm-wide traffic +1.2% was offset by conversion up 140 basis points to 30.2% and basket +5.3% to $59.10, highlighting our store-hub omnichannel pivot. Physical stores drove 35% of digital attribution, with BOPIS and ship-from-store handling 28% of e-comm as Amazon Prime Day approached.

Forward, $150 million in CapEx targets 75 remodels, favoring Southeast and Midwest for LED upgrades, new fixtures, and RFID to lift productivity 15-20%. Northeast tests include partner 'store-within-a-store' like Sherwin-Williams paint areas. Regional DCs run at 95% uptime post-Oracle WMS. These differences signal opportunities in the $850 billion home goods arena against Wayfair pressures.

3. Key strategic initiatives update: Our "Store Forward 2027" plan keeps sharpening our 1,200-plus store base, speeding omnichannel fusion, and harnessing data-led inventory control amid cooling inflation to 2.8% YoY per CPI, fading Red Sea supply issues, and rivalry from Amazon, Temu, Walmart, and Dollar General.

Across our four pillars, here's Q2 fiscal 2024 progress.

Store portfolio optimization involves curating for prime spots. We launched 18 new stores—12 in Sunbelt hotspots like Texas and Florida with 7.2% population rises per Census—and shifted three Northeast laggards hit by density and spending softness. Remodels hit 142 stores with "NextGen" designs featuring private-label experience areas, raising average tickets 9% in those versus company +3.8% comps. We closed 22 low-return sites in crowded Midwest like Ohio and Michigan with flat 0.5% SSS pre-shut. This boosted store EBITDA margins 15% in tuned units, aiming for 450 basis points system gross margin growth to 38.5% by 2027. FY2025 eyes 75 net adds, 60% Sunbelt/Southeast.

Omnichannel acceleration treats stores as the edge. BOPIS is 28% of digital sales, up from 22%, adding 12% SSS lift like Target's Drive Up. Curbside hit 15%, times down 22% to under 5 minutes via Atlanta, Dallas, Phoenix micro-fulfillment centers using Swisslog AutoStore robotics for 200+ stores, trimming digital COGS 350 basis points. HomeEssentials Rewards app has 18 million actives—65% store-tied—with Insider/Klaviyo AI personalization upping repeats 14% to 42%. West Coast at 32% omnichannel mix from tech demographics, Rust Belt at 19% getting app boosts. $2.5 billion omnichannel target is 25% of revenue this year.

Supply chain and inventory rigor counters freight easing 8% quarter-over-quarter but 20% over 2019. Zebra RFID covers 85% of stores from 45%, for 98% accuracy, 37% fewer stockouts, turns at 5.4x from 4.7x. Inventories fell 12% to $1.8 billion sans sales loss. Private labels at 32% assortments versus industry 25% per Nielsen added 520 basis points Q2 margin via Vietnam/Mexico sourcing against China tariffs. 40% apparel nearshored to El Salvador cut leads 25 days. Sunbelt turns 6.1x, Northeast seasonal excess eased by PROS dynamic pricing down markdowns 18%.

Talent and sustainability: Against 4.2% turnover, "HomeEssentials Elevate" offers $18.50/hour wages up 11%, 25,000 Coursera upskills, Legion AI scheduling dropping labor to 18.2% of sales from 19.5%. Solar on 220 roofs via SunPower meets 15% energy, saves $12 million yearly, lands Dow Jones Sustainability nod, doubles Gen Z loyalty in green areas (28% traffic).

These pillars fueled 60% of our Q2 EPS beat, setting 4-6% comps and 200 basis points EBITDA expansion for FY2025. We're pioneering brick-to-click like Home Depot SILO or Lowe's kiosks.

4. Gross margin percentage (YoY): Gross margin landed at 38.5% for the quarter—an impressive 230 basis point jump year-over-year from 36.2%—our best quarterly expansion in more than five years, validating our margin resilience program in our store-heavy operations. GAAP gross profit rose 7.2% to $1.42 billion on $3.69 billion revenue up 4.1% YoY despite traffic dips in furniture and decor. Adjusting for last year's $12 million holiday write-down, the lift was 250 basis points. Consistent across big-box (+240 bps), urban formats (+210 bps), and 15 'Essentials Express' pilots (+190 bps) tied to 2.8% comps excluding closures.

Supply chain/procurement efficiencies drove ~120 basis points: $250 million in advanced DCs like the 1.2 million sq ft Dallas-Fort Worth hub handling 25% Southern volume cut inbound freight 18% YoY despite Asia rates 15-20% high per Drewry Index. Multi-year deals with private-label partners akin to Whirlpool/Electrolux yielded 4-6% savings on fridges/washers. RFID at 85% from 45% trimmed shrink 35 bps, aged stock 22%, dodging Q4 2023 markdowns.

Product mix/private-label added 90 basis points: Own brand at 28% sales from 22%, with 500-700 bps edge. Hardlines (tools/paint/lumber) margins +310 bps to 42.1% on DIY from 1.36 million housing starts per Census. Apparel/softlines flat at 34.2% from promos vs Amazon/Walmart.

Pricing discipline contributed 60 basis points: EDLP on 65% assortments, AI PriceOptix with IRI/Nielsen optimized 12,000 SKUs vs Lowe's/Target, lifting AUR 1.9% sans volume drop—unlike Macy's 150 bps clearance loss.

Headwinds totaled 40 bps: Freight/logistics 20 bps from West port jams; 10 bps tariffs on 12% China COGS, softened by 18% Mexico apparel nearshoring. Sunbelt +280 bps on migration/remodels per CoreLogic; Northeast +150 bps from warm weather/Costco; Midwest +220 bps ag strength.

Ahead, 230 bps sets Q4 lap ease, FY target 38.7-39.1% over initial 37.0%. Omnichannel: BOPIS 14% sales, +400 bps vs pure digital. 50-store remodels +300 bps tests. 32 million loyalty up 11% grabs high-margin bundles.

This sustained expansion beats NRF retail flat margins, targeting 40%+ long-term via scale/innovation.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Thompson to provide more details on our financial results.

Sarah Thompson, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q2 2024.

Revenue: Our total revenue for the quarter was $3.0 billion, a 4.5% increase compared to the same period last year.

Gross Margin: Gross margin was 38.5%, up 230 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by supply chain efficiencies, favorable product mix shifts toward private labels, and disciplined pricing strategies.

Operating Expenses: Operating expenses were $1.75 billion, representing 58% of revenue.

Net Income: Net income was $240 million, or $1.15 per share.

Cash Flow: We generated $320 million in cash flow from operations.

Inventory: Inventory levels are currently optimized at 10 weeks' supply, down 12% year-over-year, thanks to improved turns and RFID accuracy.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of weather patterns on your regional sales variations?

Mike Hargrove, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Absolutely, weather was a notable factor, particularly in the Northeast where cool, rainy conditions suppressed outdoor categories and contributed to softer +1.8% comps. Conversely, the Southeast benefited from milder trends, fueling that standout +9.4%. Overall, our omnichannel levers like BOPIS helped mitigate these impacts across regions, keeping company comps strong at +4.2%.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Chen with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Sarah Thompson, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Emily. We're guiding to 3.5% to 5.5% same-store sales growth for Q3, supported by continued Sunbelt momentum, remodel benefits, and omnichannel ramps. This factors in potential macro softening but leverages our value positioning and inventory discipline.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Sarah, how sustainable is the gross margin expansion given freight volatility and competition?

Sarah Thompson, Chief Financial Officer:
Great question, David. The 230 basis point lift is durable, rooted in structural gains like DC investments cutting freight 18%, private-label penetration at 28%, and RFID shrink reductions. Even with headwinds like ports and tariffs, nearshoring and AI pricing provide buffers. We see 38.7-39.1% for the year, trending toward 40% long-term.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session.

Mike Hargrove, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.

Company-wide comps +4.2%, with Sunbelt outperforming traditional markets.
